notes:
I've written notes on all 24 verses below, but the research is incomplete in three ways:

- **Traditions:** none of the sources I read set Protestant traditions against each other on this passage, so part 2 is mostly empty.
- **Other views:** I didn't reach bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, or any Catholic or Orthodox commentary pages. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings.
- **Fetch failures:** the main Enduring Word and verse-by-verse Bible Hub pages wouldn't open, so the Enduring Word points come from search excerpts. The full Gill chapter page on StudyLight also failed; his notes are taken from search excerpts and Bible Hub.

Where a source names a writer's tradition, I've given it.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- "From Dan to Beersheba" means all of Israel, north to south. Gilead is the land east of the Jordan. This Mizpah is the one in Benjamin, not the Mizpah of Gilead (Constable). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-1.html
- Barnes says "unto the LORD" suggests the tabernacle was there. This Mizpah later served as a national meeting place under Samuel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-1.html
- Wesley (the page labels him Wesleyan/Methodist) reads "as one man" as "with one consent." He says "all" means a great number, especially the rulers of every tribe except Benjamin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-1.html
- Precept Austin notes that the assembly is "as one man," yet no prayer is recorded. Without asking God first, the nation reacted from its own fleshly anger. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Guzik contrasts then and now: the crime shocked Israel's conscience, but today it might just be tabloid material. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 2**
- The Hebrew word for "chiefs" means "corners" or "cornerstones." Trapp explains that leaders hold the people together the way cornerstones hold up a building. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Guzik points to Deuteronomy 13:12–18: Israel had to test whether the charges were true before acting on them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jdg/Jdg_20.cfm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott thinks Benjamin probably received the same summons as the other tribes and insolently ignored it. Pulpit says the verse shows Benjamin stayed away out of stubborn defiance, not ignorance. https://biblehub.com/judges/20-3.htm
- Benson and Poole give three reasons for Benjamin's absence: pride, the assumption that the other tribes would never go to war, and a God-sent hardening that led to their own ruin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-3.htm
- Gibeah was only about 3 miles from Mizpah, and the meeting was public, so Benjamin had every chance to respond. Precept Austin also asks whether Israel heard only the Levite and no second witness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 4**
- Gill says the Levite names "Gibeah in Benjamin" so that the other Gibeah, in Judah, would not be wrongly blamed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-1.htm (Gill excerpt via StudyLight search results)

**v. 5** (the Levite's account, a major point of discussion)
- Guzik says the Levite twisted the story in his own favour. His words were technically true, but he left out how coldly he handed his concubine to the mob. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jdg/Jdg_20.cfm
- Coffman calls it a "half-true report." The Levite talks mostly about himself and says almost nothing about the woman. Coffman also says the text of chapter 19 never says the mob meant to kill him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-5.html
- Ellicott says the Levite tells everything in the way that suits him best. Keil & Delitzsch say he worked out "they meant to kill me" from what happened to his wife, since the men never said so in 19:22. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-5.htm
- Precept Austin is the bluntest: it calls the account a lie that hides the Levite's own role in her death. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Older writers are kinder. Gill, Poole and Benson take "kill me" to mean the men would have killed him if he resisted their lust, and say he left that out out of modesty. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) calls his account plain and unexaggerated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-5.htm

**v. 6**
- The Hebrew words translated "lewd" and "disgraceful" usually describe sexual sins that deserved death. Wiersbe says the crime fits the law on rape (Deuteronomy 22:25–26) rather than adultery. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 7**
- Guzik says Israel wanted the facts so it could act on this outrage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/

**vv. 8–9**
- "As one man" comes three times in this section (vv. 1, 8, 11). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-1.html
- A Pulpit-type note on v. 18 suggests that asking God at Bethel may have been the "lot" promised in v. 9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-18.htm

**v. 10**
- Gill calculates the supply force at 40,000 out of the 400,000. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-1.htm (Gill excerpt)

**v. 11**
- Guzik says Israel rightly saw that unity is not the highest good. Unity without justice and truth is not worth having. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/

**v. 12**
- Gill thinks "tribes" here means Benjamin's ten family clans. The question was not asked to learn the facts but to make Benjamin feel how serious the crime was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-20.html
- Precept Austin says sending messengers shows Israel was looking for a way to avoid all-out war. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 13**
- Guzik says Benjamin sinned by putting loyalty to its tribe ahead of obedience to God's law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/
- Matthew Henry says that by refusing to come, Benjamin took the side of the criminals. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-13.html
- Ligonier (Reformed) says siding with Gibeah shows how far Benjamin had forgotten Israel's covenant with God. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/war-with-benjamin
- Precept Austin says Benjamin became guilty by association, almost an accomplice. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 14**
- What began as punishment of one city became full civil war, eleven tribes against one. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 15**
- Gill says 26,000 was all the fighting men Benjamin could gather. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-20.html

**v. 16**
- Clarke notes that the Hebrew for "not miss" is the ordinary word for "sin," whose basic meaning is "miss the mark." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-16.html
- Pulpit and Gill find it curious that Benjamin, whose name means "son of the right hand," had a corps of left-handed men. They connect it with Ehud (3:15). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-16.htm
- Ellicott explains the advantage: a left-handed slinger hits the enemy's unshielded right side. Poole calls "at a hair" an exaggeration meaning great accuracy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-16.htm
- Dale Ralph Davis suggests this elite unit may explain Benjamin's early victories. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Henry says Benjamin relied on its skill to make up for its smaller numbers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-16.html

**v. 17**
- Gill describes the 400,000 as skilled and courageous fighting men. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-20.html

**v. 18**
- Gill and Henry give reasons for Judah going first: it led the march in the wilderness and led the attack in Judges 1. Henry adds that Christ would come from Judah, and that the lead post was the most dangerous one. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-18.html
- Poole says Israel asked only which tribe should lead, not whether to fight, because they thought God's will on that was already clear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-18.htm
- God gave no promise of victory here. Judah may have been chosen because the concubine came from Judah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Ellicott says the answer shows the Urim and Thummim gave more than yes-or-no replies. Barnes suggests the ark may have been moved to Bethel for the occasion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-18.htm

**vv. 19–20**
- Gill notes that Israel lined up against all of Benjamin, not just the people of Gibeah. Gibeah is the very place the crime happened. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-20.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 21** (why did Israel lose?)
- Guzik offers two possibilities: they asked God but trusted their numbers and their good cause, or the defeat was God disciplining the whole nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/
- Gaebelein says Israel was self-righteous. They brought no sin offering and shed no tears of repentance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- JFB says Israel later realised it had tolerated idolatry and trusted in its numbers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-18.htm
- Benjamin's losses are not mentioned and were probably few. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 22**
- Gill says Israel took courage from its remaining numbers and its just cause. Lining up in the same place shows they held their ground and weren't superstitious about it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-20.html

**v. 23**
- Gill says Israel now doubted whether to fight its brother at all. They still didn't ask for help or victory, so none was promised. God sent them anyway because Benjamin was in the wrong and Israel had not yet been humbled enough. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-20.html
- Calling Benjamin "my brother" may mean Israel wondered whether the defeat was punishment for attacking a brother tribe. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Guzik credits Israel for weeping and seeking God after the first disaster. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/

**v. 24**
- Gill says the two battles were on consecutive days. Guzik says it shows doing right can be very costly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-20.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/

## 2. Where the traditions differ
I found no real disagreement between traditions. The actual split I found is between older and newer writers over v. 5. Older writers such as Gill (labelled Baptist on StudyLight), Poole and JFB treat the Levite's account as basically fair. Newer ones (Guzik, Coffman, Precept Austin, Ellicott) call it self-serving or partly false. The sources above have both sides.

## 3. Other views
- **The two places of worship:** the Cambridge Bible says one strand of the story places Israel's gathering at Mizpah and another at Bethel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-1.htm
- **Verse 3:** the same commentary says the first half of the verse interrupts the flow and belongs before v. 14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-3.htm
- **Verses 15–16:** in the Greek Old Testament and the Latin Vulgate, the 700 men of Gibeah are the same as the 700 left-handed slingers. Keil & Delitzsch argue they are two different groups. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-16.htm
- **Catholic translation:** the Douay-Rheims renders v. 16 as men fighting "with the left hand as well as with the right." https://biblehub.com/judges/20-16.htm
